cards.headline: Computers count in binary
lines: Digital computers store everything as bits: 0 or 1.
Eight bits make a byte — enough for 256 different values.
Text, photos and music are all patterns of bits.

cards.headline: An algorithm is a precise recipe
lines: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem.
The word comes from al-Khwarizmi, a 9th-century Persian mathematician in Baghdad.
A better algorithm can make the same job millions of times faster.
cards.source: Cormen et al., 'Introduction to Algorithms'; Knuth, 'The Art of Computer Programming', vol. 1.

cards.headline: How machine learning learns
lines: Instead of hand-written rules, a model learns patterns from many examples.
It guesses, measures its error, and nudges its settings to shrink it — over and over.
It's only as good as its data: biased examples give biased results.

cards.headline: What a language model does
lines: Large language models are trained to predict the next piece of text from what came before.
Trained on huge amounts of text, they become fluent — but fluent isn't the same as correct.
They can state false things confidently, so check anything important.
cards.source: Vaswani et al. (2017), 'Attention Is All You Need'; Brown et al. (2020), 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners'.

cards.headline: The internet runs on packets
lines: Data is split into small packets that travel separately and are reassembled on arrival.
Packets can take different routes, so the network can route around failures.
ARPANET switched to the TCP/IP rules that make this work on 1 January 1983.
cards.source: Leiner et al., 'A Brief History of the Internet' (Internet Society); Berners-Lee, 'Weaving the Web' (1999).

cards.question: How many bits are in a byte?
cards.why: Eight bits, giving 256 possible values (0 to 255).

cards.question: Who proposed the 'imitation game' — now called the Turing test — in 1950?
cards.why: Alan Turing, in 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', asked whether a machine's conversation could pass for a human's.

cards.question: Moore's law predicted that the number of transistors on a chip would…
cards.why: Gordon Moore's 1965 observation, revised in 1975 to about every two years, held for decades.
cards.source: Moore (1965), Electronics; Moore (1975), IEEE International Electron Devices Meeting.

cards.question: Ada Lovelace is often called the first computer programmer because she…
options: Published an algorithm for Babbage's engine
cards.why: Her 1843 notes on the Analytical Engine included a method for it to calculate Bernoulli numbers.
cards.source: Lovelace (1843), notes to Menabrea's 'Sketch of the Analytical Engine'.

cards.question: A chatbot gives a confident answer with a citation you can't find. What's the best move?
options: Check the claim against a reliable source
Ask it to sound more confident
cards.why: Language models can produce plausible but false details, including made-up citations. Confidence isn't evidence.
cards.source: Ji et al. (2023), 'Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation', ACM Computing Surveys.

cards.headline: The first computer 'bug' was a real moth
cards.text: In 1947, operators of the Harvard Mark II taped a moth found in a relay into their logbook. 'Bug' was already engineers' slang for a fault.
cards.source: Smithsonian National Museum of American History, the Harvard Mark II logbook.

cards.headline: Apollo flew to the Moon on tiny memory
cards.text: The Apollo Guidance Computer had about 4 KB of working memory and 72 KB of fixed program storage. A phone today has millions of times more.
cards.source: Mindell, 'Digital Apollo' (2008); MIT Instrumentation Laboratory AGC documentation.

cards.headline: QWERTY was designed for typewriters
cards.text: Christopher Latham Sholes's 1870s layout spread with the Remington typewriter — and stuck long after the mechanical reasons faded.
cards.source: Yasuoka & Yasuoka (2011), 'On the Prehistory of QWERTY', ZINBUN.

cards.headline: For passwords, length beats complexity
cards.text: US NIST guidance favours long passphrases and checks against known-breached passwords over forced symbol rules and routine resets.

cards.headline: Inside a neural network

steps.headline: 1 · Neurons
lines: An artificial neuron multiplies its inputs by weights, adds them up, and passes the total through a simple function.
On its own, it's just arithmetic.

steps.headline: 2 · Layers
lines: Neurons are stacked in layers; each layer's outputs feed the next.
Early layers find simple patterns; later layers combine them.

steps.headline: 3 · Training
lines: The network compares its output with the right answer and measures the error.
Backpropagation works out how each weight should change to shrink that error.

steps.headline: 4 · Generalising
lines: The goal is to do well on new examples, not to memorise the training set.
Testing on held-out data shows whether it really learned.

cards.source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, 'Deep Learning' (2016); Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams (1986), Nature.

cards.headline: Tech & AI: the takeaways
points: Models learn by shrinking their error.
Fluent AI isn't always correct — check it.
The internet moves data in packets.
